implementation_notes: The Kotlin stdlib supplies the mute as a value-returning construct: `runCatching { block }` calls the block and encapsulates the outcome in a Result<R>, catching any Throwable and recording it as a failure, so an ignored failure is simply the discarded Result - `.onFailure { }` keeps a breadcrumb while `.getOrNull()` turns the failure into absence. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so a plain `try { call() } catch (e: SpecificException) { }` is equally idiomatic and is the better form when exactly one narrow type should be muted, because runCatching catches everything.
pitfalls: runCatching catches Throwable, so it also swallows CancellationException - muting a coroutine cancellation breaks structured concurrency; rethrow it in onFailure or use try/catch for the narrow type instead.

A discarded Result is easy to lose: the compiler does not complain about an unused runCatching value, so the mute must read as a deliberate statement with a comment, not as an expression a later edit turns into a value.
Converting the failure to null with getOrNull() erases the reason; when the cause matters for diagnostics, keep the onFailure logging rather than turning the outcome into absence.
